summary:
Región del Libertador Bernardo O'Higgins stands under Chile's national framework. The dedicated Chile dossier published by Outright International on 12 March 2026 records no O'Higgins-specific legal, incident or enforcement finding, so this regional assessment rests on national law and on the O'Higgins row of the national case table.

National law is comparatively protective. Legal gender recognition has operated since 2019 on a self-determination basis with no medical or surgical condition attached. Same-sex marriage and joint adoption have been legal since March 2022, civil unions since 2015, and since 2012 the criminal code has treated sexual orientation and gender identity as aggravating circumstances in hate-motivated offences. Birth certificates have offered a third sex option for intersex children since 2006.

Detention carries specific protections. The national director of Gendarmería de Chile signed a protocol guaranteeing trans detainees recognition of their assumed gender, including placement and segmented housing by gender identity, entry examinations and rules on access for trans visitors; a standing committee with Gendarmería and undersecretariat representatives monitors implementation.

Regional case data is drawn from Movilh's XXIV Annual Human Rights Report (HECHOS 2025, published March 2026). Its national regional table places Libertador General Bernardo O'Higgins at 1.57% of nationally documented abuse cases in 2025, a year-on-year rise of 9.09%. Nationally the report counts 3,620 cases and complaints of discrimination in 2025, the highest total in 24 years at +27.1%; only Valparaíso (-17.56%) and Metropolitana (-14.35%) recorded falls, while the other 14 regions rose. Movilh reads the shift as hatred expanding into regions with less public debate, which is the basis for treating this region's mid-range share as a turbulence signal rather than an assurance of safety.

Policy at national level has moved against trans people. The Chilean congress excluded the Gender Identity Support Program (PAIG) from the 2026 budget bill, an action condemned by civil society groups and the national ombuds for children. Movilh's advocacy partner assessed 2024 as a year of regression for LGBTIQ+ rights, the first such reversal since the return of democracy in 1990, and the report describes a breakdown of social, political and institutional consensus around LGBTIQ+ rights, with non-discrimination law reform rejected by lawmakers.

Documented violence remains a live risk. In 2023 a young trans man, Ever, was murdered by an acquaintance and hidden for 24 hours; the case is treated as the country's benchmark anti-trans killing and was described in the national press as Chile's biggest hate crime. In September 2021 a 20-year-old trans man and his girlfriend were beaten with bottles and clubs and held against their will for close to an hour in a transphobic attack at a hotel in Santiago, during which the attacker said he wanted to kill the victim.
tangentialFactors:
The regional share must be read against the direction of travel. O'Higgins rose 9.09% in 2025 while the national total rose 27.1%, and only two of Chile's sixteen regions fell that year. A region sitting below the largest urban centres in documented cases is not thereby low-risk: Movilh's own reading is that abuse is spreading into territories with less public debate about LGBTIQ+ rights.

Comparative movement is concentrated in the two big metropolitan regions, which declined (-17.56% and -14.35%) while every other region increased. The pattern indicates displacement of recorded hostility rather than a general easing.

The national policy climate supplies the turbulence. A Chilean advocacy group's annual assessment judged 2024 a year of regression for LGBTIQ+ rights, the first since 1990, attributing the failure of equality and trans-rights bills to the rise of the ultra-right and to government inaction. Movilh's 24th report describes a breakdown of social, political and institutional consensus, with non-discrimination law reform rejected by lawmakers.

Institutional hostility is visible inside state employment. Isabella Panes, Chile's first trans police officer, sued Carabineros in 2025 alleging she was relegated to administrative duties, had her private life exposed without consent, and was denied support.
localsOnly:
Residents can change legal gender on a self-declaration basis under Gender Identity Law 21.120, in force since 2019, without medical diagnosis or surgery. Birth certificates carry a third sex option for intersex children, available since 2006.

Recognition follows into daily state contact. The Gendarmería de Chile protocol requires trans detainees to be housed according to their gender identity, with segmented housing, gender-identity-based entry examinations and rules governing access by trans visitors; a standing committee including Gendarmería and undersecretariat representatives is tasked with monitoring compliance.

Same-sex couples have been able to marry and adopt jointly since March 2022, and to register civil unions since 2015. Hate-motivated offences aggravated by the victim's sexual orientation or gender identity have been prosecutable since 2012.

For residents, the practical turn is negative on service funding: the Gender Identity Support Program (PAIG) was dropped from the 2026 budget bill by the national congress, drawing condemnation from civil society organisations and the national ombuds for children. Advocacy groups record that equality and trans-rights bills have stalled, and that non-discrimination reform was rejected.
outOfScopeNotes:
The 2024 regional share of national cases is not reproduced in the 2025 edition of the Movilh report and is therefore not sourced for this record; only the 2025 figure of 1.57% and the +9.09% change are documented here.

The Outright International Chile dossier contains no O'Higgins-specific legal, incident or enforcement material, so regional conditions are inferred from national law and from one row of a national case table. No source in this inventory addresses police treatment, health-care access, venue or bathroom access, or border and entry screening for trans visitors within this region; those remain not sourced rather than assessed.

Movilh counts cases and complaints that were documented by an advocacy organisation. The figures measure reporting and registration, not the incidence of abuse, and regional differences may reflect where complaints are lodged.

The effect on the ground of PAIG's exclusion from the 2026 budget is not documented in this inventory; only the exclusion and the condemnation it drew are sourced.
